---
title: "Strand D · Disease areas"
subtitle: "Where the biology stops being general"
---




Strands `P` and `S` are deliberately disease-agnostic. `P` teaches what a drug
does to a receptor; `S` teaches how to estimate a parameter. Neither asks what
illness is being treated, and for most of what a modeller does, neither needs to.

That generality has a limit. At some point a structural modelling decision stops
following from pharmacology and starts following from **this disease, in this
tissue, with this natural history**. Strand `D` is where those decisions live.

The organising rule is narrow, and it is what keeps this strand from becoming a
pathology textbook:

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The inclusion test
A piece of disease biology earns a place here only if it **changes a model** —
its structure, its covariates, its endpoint, or the interpretation of its
parameters. Mechanism that is fascinating but modelling-neutral belongs in a
review article, not in this curriculum.
:::

## D1 · Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma

The first disease, chosen because it fails the standard oncology modelling
playbook in an unusually instructive way. In PDAC:

- The tumour is **hypovascular and encased in dense desmoplastic stroma**, so
  the assumption that plasma exposure approximates tumour exposure — implicit in
  most exposure–response analyses — is least defensible exactly where it matters.
- The **most direct test of that idea failed**. Degrading the stromal barrier
  improved response rate and did not improve survival, in a phase 3 trial
  designed on a biomarker-selected population. That result is a better teacher
  than any successful one.
- Survival is short and tumour shrinkage is modest, which stresses the
  **tumour-size-to-survival link** that oncology pharmacometrics is built on.
- A widely used circulating biomarker, **CA19-9**, is informative, non-linear in
  its relationship to outcome, and undefined in a subset of patients for a
  reason worth understanding.

### Planned lessons

Nothing below is written yet. This is the outline, published before the prose so
the plan can be criticised before it is expensive to change — and so the
citations exist before the lessons that will rest on them.

| | Lesson | Modelling consequence | Status |

### The source material, verified

Every reference below was retrieved and checked through **PubMed** — title,
journal, year, authors and DOI. None was written from memory. Full entries are
on the [Reading](reading.qmd) page under *Strand D*.

**Disease biology.** Ying et al., *Genetics and biology of pancreatic ductal
adenocarcinoma*, Genes Dev 2025 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1101/gad.351863.124),
free full text) is the current synthesis. Wood et al., Gastroenterology 2022
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2022.03.056), free full text) covers
pathogenesis through treatment. Storz, Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2017
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrgastro.2017.12), free full text) on
acinar-to-ductal metaplasia.

**Subtypes.** Bailey et al., Nature 2016
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature16965)) — 456 tumours, 32 recurrently
mutated genes across 10 pathways, and four expression subtypes.

**Stroma.** Hosein, Brekken & Maitra, Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2020
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-020-0300-1), free full text) on the three
stromal compartments and attempts to target them. Wang et al., Biochim Biophys
Acta Rev Cancer 2019 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbcan.2019.01.007)) argues
stromal depletion is double-edged, since the stroma also restrains metastasis.

**The negative result, in two papers.** Hingorani et al., J Clin Oncol 2018
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2017.74.9564)) reported HALO-202: PFS hazard
ratio 0.73 overall and 0.51 in hyaluronan-high tumours. Van Cutsem et al., J
Clin Oncol 2020 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.20.00590), free full text)
reported HALO-109-301, the confirmatory phase 3 in 492 hyaluronan-high patients:
**objective response rate 47% versus 36%, and median overall survival 11.2
versus 11.5 months, hazard ratio 1.00.** Response improved; survival did not
move at all. `D1-07` is built on the gap between those two sentences.

**Standard of care.** Conroy et al., N Engl J Med 2011
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1011923)) — FOLFIRINOX, median OS 11.1
versus 6.8 months. Goldstein et al., J Natl Cancer Inst 2015
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/dju413)) — nab-paclitaxel plus gemcitabine,
8.7 versus 6.6 months. Wang-Gillam et al., Eur J Cancer 2019
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2018.12.007)) — liposomal irinotecan in the
second line, 6.2 versus 4.2 months.

**CA19-9.** Humphris et al., Ann Oncol 2012
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdr561), free full text).

**Gemcitabine resistance.** Ohhashi et al., Anticancer Res 2008 (PMID 18751396;
no DOI is registered for this article) on deoxycytidine kinase downregulation.

**The modelling framework.** The TGI→OS literature is not PDAC-specific and is
the backbone of `D1-11`: Claret et al., J Clin Oncol 2009
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2008.21.0807)) established the approach in
colorectal cancer; Bruno, Mercier & Claret, Clin Pharmacol Ther 2014
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/clpt.2014.4)) review which tumour-size metrics
actually predict survival; Claret et al. 2015
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-015-2820-x)) and 2016
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00280-016-3116-5)) extend it to renal cell
carcinoma and to progression-free survival.

## The therapeutic landscape, as of August 2026

The outline above was written when this disease had one story: chemotherapy with
thin margins, and a decade of targeted and immunological failures. That is no
longer the whole story, and `D1-08` and `D1-11` change because of it.

Everything in this section was retrieved and checked through **PubMed** on
30 August 2026; the regulatory details come from the **FDA** the same day.

### Chemotherapy still opens, and the margins are thin

**NAPOLI 3** (Wainberg et al., Lancet 2023
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(23)01366-1))) randomised 770 patients to
NALIRIFOX — liposomal irinotecan, oxaliplatin, leucovorin, fluorouracil — against
gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel: **median OS 11.1 versus 9.2 months, HR 0.83**.
The gain is 1.9 months, and grade ≥3 events were 87% against 86% — the toxicity is
essentially identical. FOLFIRINOX remains widely used and has never been compared
with NALIRIFOX head to head.

An adjuvant footnote worth a paragraph of `D1-08`: the **GemPred** transcriptomic
signature identified 25.5% of resected patients in PRODIGE 24 whose disease-free
and cancer-specific survival on plain adjuvant gemcitabine matched mFOLFIRINOX,
with grade ≥3 events of **40% versus 76%** (Nicolle et al., J Clin Oncol 2023
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.22.02668))). A quarter of patients may be
taking the harder regimen for no survival benefit.

### The biomarker niches are real and very small

**POLO** (Golan et al., N Engl J Med 2019
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1903387), free full text)) established
maintenance olaparib in germline *BRCA1/2*: PFS 7.4 versus 3.8 months, HR 0.53,
and **no overall survival difference** at interim — 18.9 versus 18.1 months.

The number to carry into any covariate discussion is not the hazard ratio. POLO
**screened 3,315 patients to randomise 154** — under 5%. That ratio describes the
practical ceiling on allele-specific strategies in this disease better than any
effect estimate, and it is exactly what a pan-RAS agent sidesteps.

### The KRAS turn

On **26 August 2026** the FDA granted accelerated approval to **daraxonrasib**
(RASONQUE), 300 mg orally once daily, for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma
after at least one prior systemic therapy or in patients who are not candidates
for multiagent therapy
([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/resources-information-approved-drugs/fda-approves-daraxonrasib-metastatic-pancreatic-adenocarcinoma)).
It is the first RAS inhibitor approved in this disease.

**RASolute 302** (O'Reilly et al., N Engl J Med 2026
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2605555))) randomised 500 previously treated
patients, 91.8% carrying KRAS G12 mutations:

| | Daraxonrasib | Chemotherapy | HR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median OS | **13.2 mo** | 6.6 mo | **0.40** |
| Median PFS | 7.3 mo | 3.5 mo | 0.45 |
| Objective response | 30% | 11% | — |
| Grade ≥3 adverse events | 61.8% | 69.6% | — |
| Discontinued for treatment-related events | **1.2%** | 11.2% | — |

::: {#cell-fig-pdac-os .cell fig-height='3.9' fig-width='8' execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Median overall survival by regimen and line of therapy. Cross-trial comparison — the populations differ, so this is not a formal test. The dashed rule marks the best first-line chemotherapy result; second-line daraxonrasib sits to the right of it.](diseases_files/figure-html/fig-pdac-os-output-1.png){#fig-pdac-os}
:::
:::


Daraxonrasib is a **RAS(ON) multi-selective tri-complex inhibitor**: it binds the
active GTP-bound state of mutant and wild-type H/N/KRAS rather than trapping an
inactive one, which is why it reaches G12D — the variant that dominates PDAC and
that a decade of G12C inhibitors could not touch.

Two things about that table matter more for this curriculum than the survival
number. First, second-line median OS of 13.2 months **exceeds first-line NALIRIFOX
at 11.1 months** in a different trial and population — not a formal comparison, but
the reason the field is reorganising. Second, the targeted agent was **nine times
less likely to be stopped for toxicity**, which in a disease where patients are
routinely too frail for second-line treatment is a separate kind of gain and a
separate modelling problem.

### Resistance by amplifying the target, not mutating it

The result most relevant to strand `P` is not the survival curve. Aronchik et al.
(Nat Med 2026 ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-026-04537-w))) sequenced paired
pre- and post-treatment ctDNA from 44 patients:

| Alteration at progression | Patients (of 44) |
|---|---|
| Any RAS-pathway alteration | 26 (59%) |
| **Mutant KRAS amplification** | **16 (36%)** |
| MAPK pathway | 11 (25%) |
| Receptor tyrosine kinase | 4 (9%) |
| PI3K pathway | 4 (9%) |
| **Acquired secondary KRAS mutation** | **0 (0%)** |

::: {#cell-fig-pdac-resistance .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='8' execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Treatment-emergent alterations at progression on daraxonrasib, from paired circulating tumour DNA in 44 patients. Categories are not mutually exclusive. The bottom row is the finding: it is zero.](diseases_files/figure-html/fig-pdac-resistance-output-1.png){#fig-pdac-resistance}
:::
:::


The last row is the finding, and it is categorically unlike the G12C(OFF)
inhibitors, where on-target secondary mutations are the classic escape route.
Resistance here is by *amplifying the target*, not by changing its shape.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Why this belongs in a modelling curriculum
Target amplification is a **dose-and-exposure problem, not a binding problem**. The
same plasma concentration now faces a larger target pool — which is the receptor
occupancy arithmetic of `P-04` and the target-mediated disposition of the biologics
lessons, not a new pharmacology. A curriculum that teaches occupancy and TMDD
already contains most of what is needed to reason about it, which is an unusually
direct payoff from strand `P` into a disease strand.
:::

### The pipeline behind it

| Agent | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Zoldonrasib (RMC-9805) | phase 1–2 | Covalent KRAS G12D(ON) inhibitor. Recruits cyclophilin A to form a *neomorphic* protein–protein interface that catalytically accelerates covalent reaction with the aspartate — solving the problem that carboxylic acids are weak nucleophiles and abundant proteome-wide (Weller et al., Science 2025, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ads0239)) |
| DN022150 | phase 1–2 | Selective KRAS G12D inhibitor |
| HRS-4642 + adebrelimab, or + a Nectin-4 ADC | phase 1–2 | G12D inhibitor in horizontal combination |
| Darlifarnib + adagrasib | phase 1–2 | Farnesyl transferase co-inhibition to bypass adaptive resistance in the small G12C cohort |
| Eltanexor + RAS inhibitors | **preclinical** | XPO1 inhibition to delay adaptive resistance. Xenograft and organoid data only ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218804)) |

The four clinical rows are surveyed in Pillozzi et al., J Hematol Oncol 2026
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13045-026-01834-2), free full text).

### Vaccines, and what has not worked

Personalised mRNA neoantigen vaccines are the most credible non-KRAS direction.
Autogene cevumeran induced neoantigen-specific T-cell responses in **8 of 16**
patients with resected PDAC, with recurrence delayed in immune responders — median
not reached versus 13.4 months (reported in Parganiha et al. 2026
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/23723556.2026.2652613), free full text); see also
Ye et al., Signal Transduct Target Ther 2026
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41392-026-02769-3), free full text)).

Read that carefully before repeating it: sixteen patients, half responding, and the
striking hazard ratio comes from an eight-patient subgroup defined **by response to
the intervention**. It is a hypothesis, not an effect size — and it is a good
worked example for the self-check in whichever lesson covers immortal-time and
responder bias.

What has not worked belongs here too, and `D1-07` is built on the first of these.
**Stromal depletion** improved objective response rate and did not move survival at
all in a biomarker-selected phase 3
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.20.00590)). **Checkpoint blockade as
monotherapy** is essentially inactive outside microsatellite-instability-high
disease, roughly 1% of PDAC. A curriculum that reports only successes teaches the
wrong base rate, and in this disease the base rate of failure is the single most
important fact about it.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## What this outline is not evidence of
Twenty verified citations are not twelve written lessons. The annotations above
rest on **abstracts**, not on close reading — the same standing caveat that
applies to most of the [Reading](reading.qmd) page. Publishing the outline first
is deliberate: strand `P` was written before its citations were gathered, and
the result was eighteen lessons resting on three references, which took a
separate pass to repair.
:::

## Why a third strand, rather than more lessons in P

Disease biology could have been appended to strand `P`. It is not, for two
reasons.

`P` promises to assume nothing about pharmacology and to build from first
principles. A disease deep-dive breaks that promise: it presumes the reader
already wants to model *this* indication, which most readers arriving at `P` do
not.

More practically, disease areas are the axis along which this curriculum will
grow least predictably. Keeping them in their own strand means a second disease
— immunology, a rare disease, an infectious disease — can be added without
renumbering anything, and means the inclusion test above can be applied
consistently rather than negotiated each time.

## What comes next

`D1-11` on tumour growth inhibition is the lesson most transferable to other
diseases, and `D1-07` on the stromal-depletion failure is the one with the
sharpest single teaching point. Those two are the likely starting pair.

A simulated case, `CASE-PDAC`, is the natural companion — a synthetic dataset
with published truth in the [`CASE-SM`](cases.qmd) pattern, carrying a TGI model,
a CA19-9 biomarker and a survival endpoint. It is not started.
